---
name: query
version: 1.0.0
description: |
  Answer questions using the brain's knowledge with 3-layer search, synthesis,
  and citation propagation. Use when the user asks a question, wants a lookup,
  or needs information from the brain.
triggers:
  - "what do we know about"
  - "tell me about"
  - "who is"
  - "what happened"
  - "search for"
  - "look up"
  - "background on"
  - "notes on"
  - "who knows who"
  - "relationship between"
  - "connections"
  - "graph query"
tools:
  - recall
  - search
  - query
  - get_page
  - list_pages
  - get_backlinks
  - traverse_graph
  - get_timeline
mutating: false
when_to_use: "Use when the user asks: \"what do we know about\", \"tell me about\", \"who is\", \"what happened\", \"search for\"."
---

# Query Skill

Answer questions using the brain's knowledge with 3-layer search and synthesis.

> **Memory verbs (MEMORY_VERBS v1, gbrain ≥ 0.43).** When connected to a brain
> over MCP, prefer the seven frozen memory verbs for memory work — they carry
> provenance, evidence, and a server-enforced token budget:
> - **`recall(query | entity, budget_tokens)`** — the budget-packed memory read.
>   Use it instead of bare `search` for "what do we know that we SAVED about X".
> - **`entity(name)`** — a zero-LLM person/company/project card (aliases,
>   last-touched, open threads, top edges). Use it instead of `get_page` +
>   `get_backlinks` when you just need the card.
> - **`synthesize(question)`** — the explicitly-expensive cross-page answer; the
>   heavy version of `query`. Reach for it only when the answer must combine
>   evidence across pages.
> Fall back to `search`/`query`/`get_page` when the verbs aren't on the surface
> (pre-0.43 servers; `--surface full` includes the verbs alongside every other
> op). See `docs/protocol/MEMORY_VERBS_v1.md`.

## Contract

This skill guarantees:
- Every answer is grounded in brain content (no hallucination)
- Every claim has a citation tracing back to a specific page slug
- Gaps are flagged explicitly ("the brain doesn't have information on X")
- Source precedence is respected (user statements > compiled truth > timeline > external)
- Conflicting sources are noted with both citations

## Phases

1. **Decompose the question** into search strategies:
   - Keyword search for specific names, dates, terms
   - Semantic query for conceptual questions
   - Structured queries (list by type, backlinks) for relational questions
2. **Execute searches:**
   - Cheap-hybrid search gbrain for exact tokens / known names (search)
   - Full-hybrid search gbrain for concept questions (query; `--expand` adds multi-query expansion)
   - List pages in gbrain by type or check backlinks for structural queries
   - Narrow with filters instead of grepping the brain checkout: `--types '["meeting"]'`,
     `--match keyword`, `gbrain query "<q>" --since 2026-09-01 --until 2026-09-30`, `--source <id>`.
     Every call and flag: "Which gbrain call for which lookup" in `skills/conventions/brain-first.md`.
3. **Read top results.** Read the top 3-5 pages from gbrain to get full context.
4. **Synthesize answer** with citations. Every claim traces back to a specific page slug.
5. **Flag gaps.** If the brain doesn't have info, say "the brain doesn't have information on X" rather than hallucinating. Read the result's notices first (see "When it fails"): a degraded or truncated result is not a gap.

## When it fails

Follow the [agent operator protocol](../conventions/agent-operator-protocol.md) for any gbrain error `code`, exit code, `[AGENT]` block or notice block. Specific to this skill:

- Check each retrieval result for notices before answering: on MCP, extra text blocks whose first line looks like [gbrain notice empty_retrieval kind=degraded], mirrored in `_meta.gbrain_notices`; on the CLI, the `[AGENT]` block, `search_degraded`, or a `note: search degraded` line.
- `empty_retrieval` with `kind=degraded` (or `search_degraded: keyword_only_no_embedding_provider`): an empty result is NOT proof the user has no notes. Tell the user "your brain is searching keywords only right now, so I may be missing notes on X", try exact names and synonyms with `gbrain search`, and point to the notice's fix (usually enabling embeddings).
- `empty_retrieval` with "retrieval healthy": nothing was degraded, but this one query matched nothing. Before saying "the brain doesn't have information on X", try the display name, a synonym or a hybrid search (`--match hybrid`, the default).
- `listing_truncated` or `budget_truncated`: the list was cut off. Say "showing the first N", and page or narrow the query before claiming something is absent.
- `page_not_found` from `get_page`: the slug is wrong or in another source; search by title (and check `--source`) before reporting the page missing.

## Anti-Patterns

- Answering from general knowledge when the brain has relevant content
- Hallucinating facts not in the brain
- Silently picking one source when sources conflict
- Loading full pages when search chunks are sufficient
- Ignoring source precedence (user statements are highest authority)

## Output Format

Answers should include:
- Direct response to the question
- Citations: "According to [Source: people/jane-doe, compiled truth]..."
- Gap flags: "The brain doesn't have information on X"
- Conflict notes when sources disagree

## Quality Rules

- Never hallucinate. Only answer from brain content.
- Cite sources: "According to concepts/do-things-that-dont-scale..."
- Flag stale results: if a search result shows [STALE], note that the info may be outdated
- For "who" questions, use backlinks and typed links to find connections
- For "what happened" questions, use timeline entries
- For "what do we know" questions, read compiled_truth directly

## Token-Budget Awareness

Search returns **chunks**, not full pages. Read the excerpts first before deciding
whether to load a full page.

For a question about saved **page evidence** with a tight budget, explicitly choose
`recall` with `budget_policy: "query_first"`. It gives the existing ranked page
results first use of the budget, then packs recent/filtered facts into what remains.
This is an opt-in packing choice, not a new relevance model: an irrelevant page can
displace a useful fact. Keep entity-first, session/event-filtered and fact-focused
questions on their existing facts-first route. Do not change `context_pack` or
existing third-party calls.

```bash
gbrain recall --query 'zebra telescope' --budget-tokens 75 --budget-policy query_first --json
```

Equivalent MCP request:

```json
{"name":"recall","arguments":{"query":"zebra telescope","budget_tokens":75,"budget_policy":"query_first"}}
```

**Say to your agent:** “Recall the saved notes about the zebra telescope using a
75-token estimated budget and query-first packing. Cite the returned evidence;
if the first page cannot fit, tell me rather than treating that as missing memory.”

Use the resolved brain and source as usual; the option does not widen permissions.
`budget_packing` reports the effective policy and per-arm candidate/kept/dropped/used
counts. Costs estimate `ceil(fact.length/4)` or
`ceil(title.length/4) + ceil(chunk.length/4)`, not exact tokenizer or JSON-envelope
size. Packing never skips an oversized prefix item or truncates it; multiple
required pages may still not fit. With no nonblank query or no positive finite
budget, the operation keeps legacy behavior. An eligible positive budget below one
token returns empty arms. See the protocol for fractional-budget compatibility.

This guidance and advertised tool schemas do not prove native-harness adoption.
Confirm an observed query-first call in a fresh harness conversation before
claiming activation; otherwise report adoption as unverified.

- `gbrain search` / `gbrain query` return ranked chunks with context snippets.
  These are often enough to answer the question directly.
- Hits on conversation pages (sessions, transcripts, meetings, chat logs)
  already come back as the whole session by default (`return_unit: "auto"`,
  24,000-token default budget). For other multi-page or "when did X change"
  questions, where the answer depends on the surrounding text rather than one
  chunk, ask for whole evidence in the same call: `return_unit: "page"` (whole
  page, budgeted by `token_budget`, default 6,000) or `"window"` (neighbor
  chunks). `return_unit: "chunk"` opts out.
  Each result then carries the evidence in `chunk_text` plus a `delivered`
  block; see [evidence delivery](https://github.com/garrytan/gbrain/blob/master/docs/evidence-delivery.md).
  `gbrain query "when did the launch move?" --return-unit page --token-budget 6000`
- Only use `gbrain get <slug>` to load the full page when a chunk confirms the
  page is relevant and you need more context (e.g., compiled truth, timeline).
- **"Tell me about X"** -- get the full page (the user wants the complete picture).
- **"Did anyone mention Y?"** -- search results are enough (the user wants a yes/no with evidence).

### Source precedence

When multiple sources provide conflicting information, follow this precedence:

1. **User's direct statements** (highest authority -- what the user told you directly)
2. **Compiled truth** (the brain's synthesized, cited understanding)
3. **Timeline entries** (raw evidence, reverse-chronological)
4. **External sources** (web search, API enrichment -- lowest authority)

When sources conflict, note the contradiction with both citations. Don't silently
pick one.

## Citation in Answers

When referencing brain pages in your answer, propagate inline citations:
- Cite the page: "According to [Source: people/jane-doe, compiled truth]..."
- When brain pages have inline `[Source: ...]` citations, propagate them so
  the user can trace facts to their origin
- When you synthesize across multiple pages, cite all sources

## Graph Traversal (v0.10.1+)

For relationship questions ("who knows who at X?", "connections between A and B",
"who works at Acme?", "who attended the standup?"), use the graph layer instead
of full-text search:

- `gbrain graph-query <slug> --type <link_type> --depth N --direction in|out|both`
- Available link types: `attended`, `works_at`, `invested_in`, `founded`, `advises`, `mentions`, `source`
- `--direction in` answers "who points to X?" (e.g., who works at company X)
- `--direction out` answers "what does X point to?" (default)
- `--depth N` controls multi-hop traversal (default 5)

Examples:
- "Who works at Acme?" → `gbrain graph-query companies/acme --type works_at --direction in`
- "Who attended Demo Day W26?" → `gbrain graph-query meetings/demo-day-w26 --type attended --direction out`
- "What companies has Emily advised?" → `gbrain graph-query people/emily --type advises --direction out`
- "Who has Alice met (via meetings)?" → `gbrain graph-query people/alice --type attended --depth 2`

Combine with `gbrain query` for queries that need BOTH semantic similarity AND
graph structure. Search results are ranked with a small backlink boost so well-
connected entities surface higher.

## Search Quality Awareness

If search results seem off (wrong results, missing known pages, irrelevant hits):
- Run `gbrain doctor --json` to check index health
- Check embedding coverage -- partial embeddings degrade hybrid search
- Compare keyword search (`gbrain search`) vs hybrid search (`gbrain query`)
  for the same query to isolate whether the issue is embedding-related
- Report search quality issues in the maintain workflow (see maintain skill)

## Tools Used

- Keyword search gbrain (search)
- Hybrid search gbrain (query)
- Read a page from gbrain (get_page)
- List pages in gbrain with filters (list_pages)
- Check backlinks in gbrain (get_backlinks)
- Traverse the link graph in gbrain (traverse_graph)
- View timeline entries in gbrain (get_timeline)

21	## Voluntary and involuntary disruptions
22	
23	Pods do not disappear until someone (a person or a controller) destroys them, or
24	there is an unavoidable hardware or system software error.
25	
26	We call these unavoidable cases *involuntary disruptions* to
27	an application.  Examples are:
28	
29	- a hardware failure of the physical machine backing the node
30	- cluster administrator deletes VM (instance) by mistake
31	- cloud provider or hypervisor failure makes VM disappear
32	- a kernel panic
33	- the node disappears from the cluster due to cluster network partition
34	- eviction of a pod due to the node being [out-of-resources](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/node-pressure-eviction/).
35	
36	Except for the out-of-resources condition, all these conditions
37	should be familiar to most users; they are not specific
38	to Kubernetes.
39	
40	We call other cases *voluntary disruptions*.  These include both
41	actions initiated by the application owner and those initiated by a Cluster
42	Administrator.  Typical application owner actions include:
43	
44	- deleting the deployment or other controller that manages the pod
45	- updating a deployment's pod template causing a restart
46	- directly deleting a pod (e.g. by accident)
47	
48	Cluster administrator actions include:
49	
50	- [Draining a node](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/) for repair or upgrade.
51	- Draining a node from a cluster to scale the cluster down (learn about
52	[Node Autoscaling]((/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/node-autoscaling/)).
53	- Removing a pod from a node to permit something else to fit on that node.
54	
55	These actions might be taken directly by the cluster administrator, or by automation
56	run by the cluster administrator, or by your cluster hosting provider.
57	
58	Ask your cluster administrator or consult your cloud provider or distribution documentation
59	to determine if any sources of voluntary disruptions are enabled for your cluster.
60	If none are enabled, you can skip creating Pod Disruption Budgets.
61	
62	{{< caution >}}
63	Not all voluntary disruptions are constrained by Pod Disruption Budgets. For example,
64	deleting deployments or pods bypasses Pod Disruption Budgets.
65	{{< /caution >}}
66	
67	## Dealing with disruptions
68	
69	Here are some ways to mitigate involuntary disruptions:
70	
71	- Ensure your pod [requests the resources](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/assign-memory-resource) it needs.
72	- Replicate your application if you need higher availability.  (Learn about running replicated
73	  [stateless](/docs/tasks/run-application/run-stateless-application-deployment/)
74	  and [stateful](/docs/tasks/run-application/run-replicated-stateful-application/) applications.)
75	- For even higher availability when running replicated applications,
76	  spread applications across racks (using
77	  [anti-affinity](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#affinity-and-anti-affinity))
78	  or across zones (if using a
79	  [multi-zone cluster](/docs/setup/multiple-zones).)
80	
81	The frequency of voluntary disruptions varies.  On a basic Kubernetes cluster, there are
82	no automated voluntary disruptions (only user-triggered ones).  However, your cluster administrator or hosting provider
83	may run some additional services which cause voluntary disruptions. For example,
84	rolling out node software updates can cause voluntary disruptions. Also, some implementations
85	of cluster (node) autoscaling may cause voluntary disruptions to defragment and compact nodes.
86	Your cluster administrator or hosting provider should have documented what level of voluntary
87	disruptions, if any, to expect. Certain configuration options, such as
88	[using PriorityClasses](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/pod-priority-preemption/)
89	in your pod spec can also cause voluntary (and involuntary) disruptions.
90	
91	
92	## Pod disruption budgets
93	
94	{{< feature-state for_k8s_version="v1.21" state="stable" >}}
95	
96	Kubernetes offers features to help you run highly available applications even when you
97	introduce frequent voluntary disruptions.
98	
99	As an application owner, you can create a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) for each application.
100	A PDB limits the number of Pods of a replicated application that are down simultaneously from
101	voluntary disruptions. For example, a quorum-based application would
102	like to ensure that the number of replicas running is never brought below the
103	number needed for a quorum. A web front end might want to
104	ensure that the number of replicas serving load never falls below a certain
105	percentage of the total.
106	
107	Cluster managers and hosting providers should use tools which
108	respect PodDisruptionBudgets by calling the [Eviction API](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/#eviction-api)
109	instead of directly deleting pods or deployments.
110	
111	For example, the `kubectl drain` subcommand lets you mark a node as going out of
112	service. When you run `kubectl drain`, the tool tries to evict all of the Pods on
113	the Node you're taking out of service. The eviction request that `kubectl` submits on
114	your behalf may be temporarily rejected, so the tool periodically retries all failed
115	requests until all Pods on the target node are terminated, or until a configurable timeout
116	is reached.
117	
118	A PDB specifies the number of replicas that an application can tolerate having, relative to how
119	many it is intended to have.  For example, a Deployment which has a `.spec.replicas: 5` is
120	supposed to have 5 pods at any given time.  If its PDB allows for there to be 4 at a time,
121	then the Eviction API will allow voluntary disruption of one (but not two) pods at a time.
122	
123	The group of pods that comprise the application is specified using a label selector, the same
124	as the one used by the application's controller (deployment, stateful-set, etc).
125	
126	The "intended" number of pods is computed from the `.spec.replicas` of the workload resource
127	that is managing those pods. The control plane discovers the owning workload resource by
128	examining the `.metadata.ownerReferences` of the Pod.
129	
130	[Involuntary disruptions](#voluntary-and-involuntary-disruptions) cannot be prevented by PDBs; however they
131	do count against the budget.
132	
133	Pods which are deleted or unavailable due to a rolling upgrade to an application do count
134	against the disruption budget, but workload resources (such as Deployment and StatefulSet)
135	are not limited by PDBs when doing rolling upgrades. Instead, the handling of failures
136	during application updates is configured in the spec for the specific workload resource.
137	
138	It is recommended to set `AlwaysAllow` [Unhealthy Pod Eviction Policy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#unhealthy-pod-eviction-policy)
139	to your PodDisruptionBudgets to support eviction of misbehaving applications during a node drain.
140	The default behavior is to wait for the application pods to become [healthy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#healthiness-of-a-pod)
141	before the drain can proceed.
142	
143	When a pod is evicted using the eviction API, it is gracefully
144	[terminated](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-termination), honoring the
145	`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting in its [PodSpec](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#podspec-v1-core).
146	
147	## PodDisruptionBudget example {#pdb-example}
148	
149	Consider a cluster with 3 nodes, `node-1` through `node-3`.
150	The cluster is running several applications.  One of them has 3 replicas initially called
151	`pod-a`, `pod-b`, and `pod-c`.  Another, unrelated pod without a PDB, called `pod-x`, is also shown.
152	Initially, the pods are laid out as follows:
153	
154	|       node-1         |       node-2        |       node-3       |
155	|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
156	| pod-a  *available*   | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
157	| pod-x  *available*   |                     |                    |
158	
159	All 3 pods are part of a deployment, and they collectively have a PDB which requires
160	there be at least 2 of the 3 pods to be available at all times.
161	
162	For example, assume the cluster administrator wants to reboot into a new kernel version to fix a bug in the kernel.
163	The cluster administrator first tries to drain `node-1` using the `kubectl drain` command.
164	That tool tries to evict `pod-a` and `pod-x`.  This succeeds immediately.
165	Both pods go into the `terminating` state at the same time.
166	This puts the cluster in this state:
167	
168	|   node-1 *draining*  |       node-2        |       node-3       |
169	|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
170	| pod-a  *terminating* | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
171	| pod-x  *terminating* |                     |                    |
172	
173	The deployment notices that one of the pods is terminating, so it creates a replacement
174	called `pod-d`.  Since `node-1` is cordoned, it lands on another node.  Something has
175	also created `pod-y` as a replacement for `pod-x`.
176	
177	(Note: for a StatefulSet, `pod-a`, which would be called something like `pod-0`, would need
178	to terminate completely before its replacement, which is also called `pod-0` but has a
179	different UID, could be created.  Otherwise, the example applies to a StatefulSet as well.)
180	
181	Now the cluster is in this state:
182	
183	|   node-1 *draining*  |       node-2        |       node-3       |
184	|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
185	| pod-a  *terminating* | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
186	| pod-x  *terminating* | pod-d *starting*    | pod-y              |
187	
188	At some point, the pods terminate, and the cluster looks like this:
189	
190	|    node-1 *drained*  |       node-2        |       node-3       |
191	|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
192	|                      | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
193	|                      | pod-d *starting*    | pod-y              |
194	
195	At this point, if an impatient cluster administrator tries to drain `node-2` or
196	`node-3`, the drain command will block, because there are only 2 available
197	pods for the deployment, and its PDB requires at least 2.  After some time passes, `pod-d` becomes available.
198	
199	The cluster state now looks like this:
200	
201	|    node-1 *drained*  |       node-2        |       node-3       |
202	|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
203	|                      | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
204	|                      | pod-d *available*   | pod-y              |
205	
206	Now, the cluster administrator tries to drain `node-2`.
207	The drain command will try to evict the two pods in some order, say
208	`pod-b` first and then `pod-d`.  It will succeed at evicting `pod-b`.
209	But, when it tries to evict `pod-d`, it will be refused because that would leave only
210	one pod available for the deployment.
211	
212	The deployment creates a replacement for `pod-b` called `pod-e`.
213	Because there are not enough resources in the cluster to schedule
214	`pod-e` the drain will again block.  The cluster may end up in this
215	state:
216	
217	|    node-1 *drained*  |       node-2        |       node-3       | *no node*          |
218	|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|:------------------:|
219	|                      | pod-b *terminating* | pod-c *available*  | pod-e *pending*    |

## Voluntary and involuntary disruptions

Pods do not disappear until someone (a person or a controller) destroys them, or
there is an unavoidable hardware or system software error.

We call these unavoidable cases *involuntary disruptions* to
an application.  Examples are:

- a hardware failure of the physical machine backing the node
- cluster administrator deletes VM (instance) by mistake
- cloud provider or hypervisor failure makes VM disappear
- a kernel panic
- the node disappears from the cluster due to cluster network partition
- eviction of a pod due to the node being [out-of-resources](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/node-pressure-eviction/).

Except for the out-of-resources condition, all these conditions
should be familiar to most users; they are not specific
to Kubernetes.

We call other cases *voluntary disruptions*.  These include both
actions initiated by the application owner and those initiated by a Cluster
Administrator.  Typical application owner actions include:

- deleting the deployment or other controller that manages the pod
- updating a deployment's pod template causing a restart
- directly deleting a pod (e.g. by accident)

Cluster administrator actions include:

- [Draining a node](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/) for repair or upgrade.
- Draining a node from a cluster to scale the cluster down (learn about
[Node Autoscaling]((/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/node-autoscaling/)).
- Removing a pod from a node to permit something else to fit on that node.

These actions might be taken directly by the cluster administrator, or by automation
run by the cluster administrator, or by your cluster hosting provider.

Ask your cluster administrator or consult your cloud provider or distribution documentation
to determine if any sources of voluntary disruptions are enabled for your cluster.
If none are enabled, you can skip creating Pod Disruption Budgets.

{{< caution >}}
Not all voluntary disruptions are constrained by Pod Disruption Budgets. For example,
deleting deployments or pods bypasses Pod Disruption Budgets.
{{< /caution >}}

## Dealing with disruptions

Here are some ways to mitigate involuntary disruptions:

- Ensure your pod [requests the resources](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/assign-memory-resource) it needs.
- Replicate your application if you need higher availability.  (Learn about running replicated
  [stateless](/docs/tasks/run-application/run-stateless-application-deployment/)
  and [stateful](/docs/tasks/run-application/run-replicated-stateful-application/) applications.)
- For even higher availability when running replicated applications,
  spread applications across racks (using
  [anti-affinity](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#affinity-and-anti-affinity))
  or across zones (if using a
  [multi-zone cluster](/docs/setup/multiple-zones).)

The frequency of voluntary disruptions varies.  On a basic Kubernetes cluster, there are
no automated voluntary disruptions (only user-triggered ones).  However, your cluster administrator or hosting provider
may run some additional services which cause voluntary disruptions. For example,
rolling out node software updates can cause voluntary disruptions. Also, some implementations
of cluster (node) autoscaling may cause voluntary disruptions to defragment and compact nodes.
Your cluster administrator or hosting provider should have documented what level of voluntary
disruptions, if any, to expect. Certain configuration options, such as
[using PriorityClasses](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/pod-priority-preemption/)
in your pod spec can also cause voluntary (and involuntary) disruptions.


## Pod disruption budgets

{{< feature-state for_k8s_version="v1.21" state="stable" >}}

Kubernetes offers features to help you run highly available applications even when you
introduce frequent voluntary disruptions.

As an application owner, you can create a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) for each application.
A PDB limits the number of Pods of a replicated application that are down simultaneously from
voluntary disruptions. For example, a quorum-based application would
like to ensure that the number of replicas running is never brought below the
number needed for a quorum. A web front end might want to
ensure that the number of replicas serving load never falls below a certain
percentage of the total.

Cluster managers and hosting providers should use tools which
respect PodDisruptionBudgets by calling the [Eviction API](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/#eviction-api)
instead of directly deleting pods or deployments.

For example, the `kubectl drain` subcommand lets you mark a node as going out of
service. When you run `kubectl drain`, the tool tries to evict all of the Pods on
the Node you're taking out of service. The eviction request that `kubectl` submits on
your behalf may be temporarily rejected, so the tool periodically retries all failed
requests until all Pods on the target node are terminated, or until a configurable timeout
is reached.

A PDB specifies the number of replicas that an application can tolerate having, relative to how
many it is intended to have.  For example, a Deployment which has a `.spec.replicas: 5` is
supposed to have 5 pods at any given time.  If its PDB allows for there to be 4 at a time,
then the Eviction API will allow voluntary disruption of one (but not two) pods at a time.

The group of pods that comprise the application is specified using a label selector, the same
as the one used by the application's controller (deployment, stateful-set, etc).

The "intended" number of pods is computed from the `.spec.replicas` of the workload resource
that is managing those pods. The control plane discovers the owning workload resource by
examining the `.metadata.ownerReferences` of the Pod.

[Involuntary disruptions](#voluntary-and-involuntary-disruptions) cannot be prevented by PDBs; however they
do count against the budget.

Pods which are deleted or unavailable due to a rolling upgrade to an application do count
against the disruption budget, but workload resources (such as Deployment and StatefulSet)
are not limited by PDBs when doing rolling upgrades. Instead, the handling of failures
during application updates is configured in the spec for the specific workload resource.

It is recommended to set `AlwaysAllow` [Unhealthy Pod Eviction Policy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#unhealthy-pod-eviction-policy)
to your PodDisruptionBudgets to support eviction of misbehaving applications during a node drain.
The default behavior is to wait for the application pods to become [healthy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#healthiness-of-a-pod)
before the drain can proceed.

When a pod is evicted using the eviction API, it is gracefully
[terminated](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-termination), honoring the
`terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting in its [PodSpec](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#podspec-v1-core).

## PodDisruptionBudget example {#pdb-example}

Consider a cluster with 3 nodes, `node-1` through `node-3`.
The cluster is running several applications.  One of them has 3 replicas initially called
`pod-a`, `pod-b`, and `pod-c`.  Another, unrelated pod without a PDB, called `pod-x`, is also shown.
Initially, the pods are laid out as follows:

|       node-1         |       node-2        |       node-3       |
|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
| pod-a  *available*   | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
| pod-x  *available*   |                     |                    |

All 3 pods are part of a deployment, and they collectively have a PDB which requires
there be at least 2 of the 3 pods to be available at all times.

For example, assume the cluster administrator wants to reboot into a new kernel version to fix a bug in the kernel.
The cluster administrator first tries to drain `node-1` using the `kubectl drain` command.
That tool tries to evict `pod-a` and `pod-x`.  This succeeds immediately.
Both pods go into the `terminating` state at the same time.
This puts the cluster in this state:

|   node-1 *draining*  |       node-2        |       node-3       |
|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
| pod-a  *terminating* | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
| pod-x  *terminating* |                     |                    |

The deployment notices that one of the pods is terminating, so it creates a replacement
called `pod-d`.  Since `node-1` is cordoned, it lands on another node.  Something has
also created `pod-y` as a replacement for `pod-x`.

(Note: for a StatefulSet, `pod-a`, which would be called something like `pod-0`, would need
to terminate completely before its replacement, which is also called `pod-0` but has a
different UID, could be created.  Otherwise, the example applies to a StatefulSet as well.)

Now the cluster is in this state:

|   node-1 *draining*  |       node-2        |       node-3       |
|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
| pod-a  *terminating* | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
| pod-x  *terminating* | pod-d *starting*    | pod-y              |

At some point, the pods terminate, and the cluster looks like this:

|    node-1 *drained*  |       node-2        |       node-3       |
|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
|                      | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
|                      | pod-d *starting*    | pod-y              |

At this point, if an impatient cluster administrator tries to drain `node-2` or
`node-3`, the drain command will block, because there are only 2 available
pods for the deployment, and its PDB requires at least 2.  After some time passes, `pod-d` becomes available.

The cluster state now looks like this:

|    node-1 *drained*  |       node-2        |       node-3       |
|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|
|                      | pod-b *available*   | pod-c *available*  |
|                      | pod-d *available*   | pod-y              |

Now, the cluster administrator tries to drain `node-2`.
The drain command will try to evict the two pods in some order, say
`pod-b` first and then `pod-d`.  It will succeed at evicting `pod-b`.
But, when it tries to evict `pod-d`, it will be refused because that would leave only
one pod available for the deployment.

The deployment creates a replacement for `pod-b` called `pod-e`.
Because there are not enough resources in the cluster to schedule
`pod-e` the drain will again block.  The cluster may end up in this
state:

|    node-1 *drained*  |       node-2        |       node-3       | *no node*          |
|:--------------------:|:-------------------:|:------------------:|:------------------:|
|                      | pod-b *terminating* | pod-c *available*  | pod-e *pending*    |

300	[PodConditions](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#podcondition-v1-core)
301	through which the Pod has or has not passed. Kubelet manages the following
302	PodConditions:
303	
304	* `PodScheduled`: the Pod has been scheduled to a node.
305	* `PodReadyToStartContainers`: (beta feature; enabled by [default](#pod-has-network)) the
306	  Pod sandbox has been successfully created and networking configured.
307	* `ContainersReady`: all containers in the Pod are ready.
308	* `Initialized`: all [init containers](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/init-containers/)
309	  have completed successfully.
310	* `Ready`: the Pod is able to serve requests and should be added to the load
311	  balancing pools of all matching Services.
312	
313	Field name           | Description
314	:--------------------|:-----------
315	`type`               | Name of this Pod condition.
316	`status`             | Indicates whether that condition is applicable, with possible values "`True`", "`False`", or "`Unknown`".
317	`lastProbeTime`      | Timestamp of when the Pod condition was last probed.
318	`lastTransitionTime` | Timestamp for when the Pod last transitioned from one status to another.
319	`reason`             | Machine-readable, UpperCamelCase text indicating the reason for the condition's last transition.
320	`message`            | Human-readable message indicating details about the last status transition.
321	
322	
323	### Pod readiness {#pod-readiness-gate}
324	
325	{{< feature-state for_k8s_version="v1.14" state="stable" >}}
326	
327	Your application can inject extra feedback or signals into PodStatus:
328	_Pod readiness_. To use this, set `readinessGates` in the Pod's `spec` to

423	
424	A _probe_ is a diagnostic performed periodically by the [kubelet](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kubelet/)

430	There are four different ways to check a container using a probe.

441	  The diagnostic is considered successful if the `status`
442	  of the response is `SERVING`.

447	  considered successful if the response has a status code
448	  greater than or equal to 200 and less than 400.

451	: Performs a TCP check against the Pod's IP address on
452	  a specified port. The diagnostic is considered successful if
453	  the port is open. If the remote system (the container) closes
454	  the connection immediately after it opens, this counts as healthy.

1. The kubelet ensures the Pod is shut down and terminated

      kubelet triggers forcible shutdown.
      The container runtime sends `SIGKILL` to any processes still running in any container in the Pod.

   1. The kubelet transitions the Pod into a terminal phase (`Failed` or `Succeeded` depending on

### Forced Pod termination {#pod-termination-forced}

{{< caution >}}
Forced deletions can be potentially disruptive for some workloads and their Pods.
{{< /caution >}}

By default, all deletes are graceful within 30 seconds. The `kubectl delete` command supports
the `--grace-period=<seconds>` option which allows you to override the default and specify your
own value.

Setting the grace period to `0` forcibly and immediately deletes the Pod from the API

76	### Spread constraint definition
77	
78	You can define one or multiple `topologySpreadConstraints` entries to instruct the
79	kube-scheduler how to place each incoming Pod in relation to the existing Pods across
80	your cluster. Those fields are:
81	
82	- **maxSkew** describes the degree to which Pods may be unevenly distributed. You must
83	  specify this field and the number must be greater than zero. Its semantics differ
84	  according to the value of `whenUnsatisfiable`:
85	
86	  - if you select `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule`, then `maxSkew` defines the
87	    maximum permitted difference between the number of matching pods in the target
88	    topology and the _global minimum_
89	    (the minimum number of matching pods in an eligible domain or zero if the number of eligible domains is less than MinDomains).
90	    For example, if you have 3 zones with 2, 2 and 1 matching pods respectively,
91	    `MaxSkew` is set to 1 then the global minimum is 1.
92	  - if you select `whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway`, the scheduler gives higher
93	    precedence to topologies that would help reduce the skew.
94	
95	- **minDomains** indicates a minimum number of eligible domains. This field is optional.
96	  A domain is a particular instance of a topology. An eligible domain is a domain whose
97	  nodes match the node selector.
98	
99	  <!-- OK to remove this note once v1.29 Kubernetes is out of support -->
100	  {{< note >}}
101	  Before Kubernetes v1.30, the `minDomains` field was only available if the
102	  `MinDomainsInPodTopologySpread` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates-removed/)
103	  was enabled (default since v1.28). In older Kubernetes clusters it might be explicitly
104	  disabled or the field might not be available.
105	  {{< /note >}}
106	
107	  - The value of `minDomains` must be greater than 0, when specified.
108	    You can only specify `minDomains` in conjunction with `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule`.
109	  - When the number of eligible domains with match topology keys is less than `minDomains`,
110	    Pod topology spread treats global minimum as 0, and then the calculation of `skew` is performed.
111	    The global minimum is the minimum number of matching Pods in an eligible domain,
112	    or zero if the number of eligible domains is less than `minDomains`.
113	  - When the number of eligible domains with matching topology keys equals or is greater than
114	    `minDomains`, this value has no effect on scheduling.
115	  - If you do not specify `minDomains`, the constraint behaves as if `minDomains` is 1.
116	
117	- **topologyKey** is the key of [node labels](#node-labels). Nodes that have a label with this key
118		and identical values are considered to be in the same topology.
119	  We call each instance of a topology (in other words, a <key, value> pair) a domain. The scheduler
120	  will try to put a balanced number of pods into each domain.
121		Also, we define an eligible domain as a domain whose nodes meet the requirements of
122		nodeAffinityPolicy and nodeTaintsPolicy.
123	
124	- **whenUnsatisfiable** indicates how to deal with a Pod if it doesn't satisfy the spread constraint:
125	  - `DoNotSchedule` (default) tells the scheduler not to schedule it.
126	  - `ScheduleAnyway` tells the scheduler to still schedule it while prioritizing nodes that minimize the skew.
127	
128	- **labelSelector** is used to find matching Pods. Pods
129	  that match this label selector are counted to determine the
130	  number of Pods in their corresponding topology domain.
131	  See [Label Selectors](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#label-selectors)
132	  for more details.
133	
134	- **matchLabelKeys** is a list of pod label keys to select the pods over which
135	  spreading will be calculated. The keys are used to lookup values from the pod labels,
136	  those key-value labels are ANDed with `labelSelector` to select the group of existing
137	  pods over which spreading will be calculated for the incoming pod. The same key is
138	  forbidden to exist in both `matchLabelKeys` and `labelSelector`. `matchLabelKeys` cannot
139	  be set when `labelSelector` isn't set. Keys that don't exist in the pod labels will be
140	  ignored. A null or empty list means only match against the `labelSelector`.
141	
142	  With `matchLabelKeys`, you don't need to update the `pod.spec` between different revisions.
143	  The controller/operator just needs to set different values to the same label key for different
144	  revisions. The scheduler will assume the values automatically based on `matchLabelKeys`. For
145	  example, if you are configuring a Deployment, you can use the label keyed with
146	  [pod-template-hash](/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#pod-template-hash-label), which
147	  is added automatically by the Deployment controller, to distinguish between different revisions
148	  in a single Deployment.

153	            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname

# Configure a topology spread constraint
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: <integer>
      minDomains: <integer> # optional
      topologyKey: <string>
      whenUnsatisfiable: <string>
      labelSelector: <object>
      matchLabelKeys: <list> # optional; beta since v1.27
      nodeAffinityPolicy: [Honor|Ignore] # optional; beta since v1.26
      nodeTaintsPolicy: [Honor|Ignore] # optional; beta since v1.26
  ### other Pod fields go here
```

You can read more about this field by running `kubectl explain Pod.spec.topologySpreadConstraints` or
refer to the [scheduling](/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1/#scheduling) section of the API reference for Pod.

### Spread constraint definition

You can define one or multiple `topologySpreadConstraints` entries to instruct the
kube-scheduler how to place each incoming Pod in relation to the existing Pods across
your cluster. Those fields are:

- **maxSkew** describes the degree to which Pods may be unevenly distributed. You must
  specify this field and the number must be greater than zero. Its semantics differ
  according to the value of `whenUnsatisfiable`:

  - if you select `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule`, then `maxSkew` defines the
    maximum permitted difference between the number of matching pods in the target
    topology and the _global minimum_
    (the minimum number of matching pods in an eligible domain or zero if the number of eligible domains is less than MinDomains).
    For example, if you have 3 zones with 2, 2 and 1 matching pods respectively,
    `MaxSkew` is set to 1 then the global minimum is 1.
  - if you select `whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway`, the scheduler gives higher
    precedence to topologies that would help reduce the skew.

- **minDomains** indicates a minimum number of eligible domains. This field is optional.
  A domain is a particular instance of a topology. An eligible domain is a domain whose
  nodes match the node selector.

  <!-- OK to remove this note once v1.29 Kubernetes is out of support -->
  {{< note >}}
  Before Kubernetes v1.30, the `minDomains` field was only available if the
  `MinDomainsInPodTopologySpread` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates-removed/)
  was enabled (default since v1.28). In older Kubernetes clusters it might be explicitly
  disabled or the field might not be available.
  {{< /note >}}

  - The value of `minDomains` must be greater than 0, when specified.
    You can only specify `minDomains` in conjunction with `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule`.
  - When the number of eligible domains with match topology keys is less than `minDomains`,
    Pod topology spread treats global minimum as 0, and then the calculation of `skew` is performed.
    The global minimum is the minimum number of matching Pods in an eligible domain,
    or zero if the number of eligible domains is less than `minDomains`.
  - When the number of eligible domains with matching topology keys equals or is greater than
    `minDomains`, this value has no effect on scheduling.
  - If you do not specify `minDomains`, the constraint behaves as if `minDomains` is 1.

- **topologyKey** is the key of [node labels](#node-labels). Nodes that have a label with this key
	and identical values are considered to be in the same topology.
  We call each instance of a topology (in other words, a <key, value> pair) a domain. The scheduler
  will try to put a balanced number of pods into each domain.
	Also, we define an eligible domain as a domain whose nodes meet the requirements of
	nodeAffinityPolicy and nodeTaintsPolicy.

- **whenUnsatisfiable** indicates how to deal with a Pod if it doesn't satisfy the spread constraint:
  - `DoNotSchedule` (default) tells the scheduler not to schedule it.
  - `ScheduleAnyway` tells the scheduler to still schedule it while prioritizing nodes that minimize the skew.

- **labelSelector** is used to find matching Pods. Pods
  that match this label selector are counted to determine the
  number of Pods in their corresponding topology domain.
  See [Label Selectors](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/#label-selectors)
  for more details.

- **matchLabelKeys** is a list of pod label keys to select the pods over which
  spreading will be calculated. The keys are used to lookup values from the pod labels,
  those key-value labels are ANDed with `labelSelector` to select the group of existing
  pods over which spreading will be calculated for the incoming pod. The same key is
  forbidden to exist in both `matchLabelKeys` and `labelSelector`. `matchLabelKeys` cannot
  be set when `labelSelector` isn't set. Keys that don't exist in the pod labels will be
  ignored. A null or empty list means only match against the `labelSelector`.

  With `matchLabelKeys`, you don't need to update the `pod.spec` between different revisions.
  The controller/operator just needs to set different values to the same label key for different
  revisions. The scheduler will assume the values automatically based on `matchLabelKeys`. For
  example, if you are configuring a Deployment, you can use the label keyed with
  [pod-template-hash](/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#pod-template-hash-label), which
  is added automatically by the Deployment controller, to distinguish between different revisions
  in a single Deployment.

  ```yaml
      topologySpreadConstraints:
          - maxSkew: 1
            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
            whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
            labelSelector:
              matchLabels:
                app: foo
            matchLabelKeys:
              - pod-template-hash
  ```

  {{< note >}}
  The `matchLabelKeys` field is a beta-level field and enabled by default in 1.27. You can disable it by disabling the
  `MatchLabelKeysInPodTopologySpread` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/).
  {{< /note >}}

- **nodeAffinityPolicy** indicates how we will treat Pod's nodeAffinity/nodeSelector
  when calculating pod topology spread skew. Options are:
  - Honor: only nodes matching nodeAffinity/nodeSelector are included in the calculations.
  - Ignore: nodeAffinity/nodeSelector are ignored. All nodes are included in the calculations.

  If this value is null, the behavior is equivalent to the Honor policy.

  {{< note >}}
  The `nodeAffinityPolicy` is a beta-level field and enabled by default in 1.26. You can disable it by disabling the
  `NodeInclusionPolicyInPodTopologySpread` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/).
  {{< /note >}}

- **nodeTaintsPolicy** indicates how we will treat node taints when calculating
  pod topology spread skew. Options are:
  - Honor: nodes without taints, along with tainted nodes for which the incoming pod
    has a toleration, are included.
  - Ignore: node taints are ignored. All nodes are included.

  If this value is null, the behavior is equivalent to the Ignore policy.

  {{< note >}}
  The `nodeTaintsPolicy` is a beta-level field and enabled by default in 1.26. You can disable it by disabling the
  `NodeInclusionPolicyInPodTopologySpread` [feature gate](/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/feature-gates/).
  {{< /note >}}

When a Pod defines more than one `topologySpreadConstraint`, those constraints are
combined using a logical AND operation: the kube-scheduler looks for a node for the incoming Pod
that satisfies all the configured constraints.

### Node labels

Topology spread constraints rely on node labels to identify the topology
domain(s) that each {{< glossary_tooltip text="node" term_id="node" >}} is in.
For example, a node might have labels:
```yaml
  region: us-east-1
  zone: us-east-1a
```

{{< note >}}
For brevity, this example doesn't use the
[well-known](/docs/reference/labels-annotations-taints/) label keys
`topology.kubernetes.io/zone` and `topology.kubernetes.io/region`. However,

   541	  - maxSkew: 3
   542	    topologyKey: "kubernetes.io/hostname"
   543	    whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
   544	  - maxSkew: 5
   545	    topologyKey: "topology.kubernetes.io/zone"
   546	    whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway

   548	
   549	Also, the legacy `SelectorSpread` plugin, which provides an equivalent behavior,
   550	is disabled by default.
   551	
   552	{{< note >}}
   553	The `PodTopologySpread` plugin does not score the nodes that don't have
   554	the topology keys specified in the spreading constraints. This might result
   555	in a different default behavior compared to the legacy `SelectorSpread` plugin when
   556	using the default topology constraints.
   557	
   558	If your nodes are not expected to have **both** `kubernetes.io/hostname` and
   559	`topology.kubernetes.io/zone` labels set, define your own constraints
   560	instead of using the Kubernetes defaults.
   561	{{< /note >}}
   562	
   563	If you don't want to use the default Pod spreading constraints for your cluster,
   564	you can disable those defaults by setting `defaultingType` to `List` and leaving
   565	empty `defaultConstraints` in the `PodTopologySpread` plugin configuration:
   566	
   567	```yaml
   568	apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1
   569	kind: KubeSchedulerConfiguration
   570	
   571	profiles:
   572	  - schedulerName: default-scheduler
   573	    pluginConfig:
   574	      - name: PodTopologySpread
   575	        args:
   576	          defaultConstraints: []
   577	          defaultingType: List
   578	```
   579	
   580	## Comparison with podAffinity and podAntiAffinity {#comparison-with-podaffinity-podantiaffinity}
   581	
   582	In Kubernetes, [inter-Pod affinity and anti-affinity](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#inter-pod-affinity-and-anti-affinity)
   583	control how Pods are scheduled in relation to one another - either more packed
   584	or more scattered.
   585	
   586	`podAffinity`
   587	: attracts Pods; you can try to pack any number of Pods into qualifying
   588	  topology domain(s).
   589	
   590	`podAntiAffinity`
   591	: repels Pods. If you set this to `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` mode then
   592	  only a single Pod can be scheduled into a single topology domain; if you choose
   593	  `preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` then you lose the ability to enforce the
   594	  constraint.
   595	
   596	For finer control, you can specify topology spread constraints to distribute
   597	Pods across different topology domains - to achieve either high availability or
   598	cost-saving. This can also help on rolling update workloads and scaling out
   599	replicas smoothly.
   600	
   601	For more context, see the
   602	[Motivation](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-scheduling/895-pod-topology-spread#motivation)
   603	section of the enhancement proposal about Pod topology spread constraints.
   604	
   605	## Known limitations
   606	
   607	- There's no guarantee that the constraints remain satisfied when Pods are removed. For
   608	  example, scaling down a Deployment may result in imbalanced Pods distribution.
   609	
   610	  You can use a tool such as the [Descheduler](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/descheduler)
   611	  to rebalance the Pods distribution.
   612	- Pods matched on tainted nodes are respected.
   613	  See [Issue 80921](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/80921).
   614	- The scheduler doesn't have prior knowledge of all the zones or other topology
   615	  domains that a cluster has. They are determined from the existing nodes in the
   616	  cluster. This could lead to a problem in autoscaled clusters, when a node pool (or
   617	  node group) is scaled to zero nodes, and you're expecting the cluster to scale up,
   618	  because, in this case, those topology domains won't be considered until there is
   619	  at least one node in them.

   560	instead of using the Kubernetes defaults.
   561	{{< /note >}}
   562	
   563	If you don't want to use the default Pod spreading constraints for your cluster,
   564	you can disable those defaults by setting `defaultingType` to `List` and leaving
   565	empty `defaultConstraints` in the `PodTopologySpread` plugin configuration:
   566	
   567	```yaml
   568	apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1
   569	kind: KubeSchedulerConfiguration
   570	
   571	profiles:
   572	  - schedulerName: default-scheduler
   573	    pluginConfig:
   574	      - name: PodTopologySpread
   575	        args:
   576	          defaultConstraints: []
   577	          defaultingType: List
   578	```
   579	
   580	## Comparison with podAffinity and podAntiAffinity {#comparison-with-podaffinity-podantiaffinity}
   581	
   582	In Kubernetes, [inter-Pod affinity and anti-affinity](/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#inter-pod-affinity-and-anti-affinity)
   583	control how Pods are scheduled in relation to one another - either more packed
   584	or more scattered.
   585	
   586	`podAffinity`
   587	: attracts Pods; you can try to pack any number of Pods into qualifying
   588	  topology domain(s).
   589	
   590	`podAntiAffinity`
   591	: repels Pods. If you set this to `requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` mode then
   592	  only a single Pod can be scheduled into a single topology domain; if you choose
   593	  `preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution` then you lose the ability to enforce the
   594	  constraint.
   595	
   596	For finer control, you can specify topology spread constraints to distribute
   597	Pods across different topology domains - to achieve either high availability or
   598	cost-saving. This can also help on rolling update workloads and scaling out
   599	replicas smoothly.
   600	
   601	For more context, see the
   602	[Motivation](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-scheduling/895-pod-topology-spread#motivation)
   603	section of the enhancement proposal about Pod topology spread constraints.
   604	
   605	## Known limitations
   606	
   607	- There's no guarantee that the constraints remain satisfied when Pods are removed. For
   608	  example, scaling down a Deployment may result in imbalanced Pods distribution.
   609	
   610	  You can use a tool such as the [Descheduler](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/descheduler)
   611	  to rebalance the Pods distribution.
   612	- Pods matched on tainted nodes are respected.
   613	  See [Issue 80921](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/80921).
   614	- The scheduler doesn't have prior knowledge of all the zones or other topology
   615	  domains that a cluster has. They are determined from the existing nodes in the
   616	  cluster. This could lead to a problem in autoscaled clusters, when a node pool (or
   617	  node group) is scaled to zero nodes, and you're expecting the cluster to scale up,
   618	  because, in this case, those topology domains won't be considered until there is
   619	  at least one node in them.

  1091	
  1092	## Canary Deployment
  1093	
  1094	If you want to roll out releases to a subset of users or servers using the Deployment, you
  1095	can create multiple Deployments, one for each release, following the canary pattern described in
  1096	[managing resources](/docs/concepts/workloads/management/#canary-deployments).
  1097	
  1098	## Writing a Deployment Spec
  1099	
  1100	As with all other Kubernetes configs, a Deployment needs `.apiVersion`, `.kind`, and `.metadata` fields.
  1101	For general information about working with config files, see
  1102	[deploying applications](/docs/tasks/run-application/run-stateless-application-deployment/),
  1103	configuring containers, and [using kubectl to manage resources](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/object-management/) documents.
  1104	
  1105	When the control plane creates new Pods for a Deployment, the `.metadata.name` of the
  1106	Deployment is part of the basis for naming those Pods. The name of a Deployment must be a valid
  1107	[DNS subdomain](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/names#dns-subdomain-names)
  1108	value, but this can produce unexpected results for the Pod hostnames. For best compatibility,
  1109	the name should follow the more restrictive rules for a
  1110	[DNS label](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/names#dns-label-names).
  1111	
  1112	A Deployment also needs a [`.spec` section](https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md#spec-and-status).
  1113	
  1114	### Pod Template
  1115	
  1116	The `.spec.template` and `.spec.selector` are the only required fields of the `.spec`.
  1117	
  1118	The `.spec.template` is a [Pod template](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/#pod-templates). It has exactly the same schema as a {{< glossary_tooltip text="Pod" term_id="pod" >}}, except it is nested and does not have an `apiVersion` or `kind`.
  1119	
  1120	In addition to required fields for a Pod, a Pod template in a Deployment must specify appropriate
  1121	labels and an appropriate restart policy. For labels, make sure not to overlap with other controllers. See [selector](#selector).
  1122	
  1123	Only a [`.spec.template.spec.restartPolicy`](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#restart-policy) equal to `Always` is
  1124	allowed, which is the default if not specified.
  1125	
  1126	### Replicas
  1127	
  1128	`.spec.replicas` is an optional field that specifies the number of desired Pods. It defaults to 1.
  1129	
  1130	Should you manually scale a Deployment, example via `kubectl scale deployment
  1131	deployment --replicas=X`, and then you update that Deployment based on a manifest
  1132	(for example: by running `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml`),
  1133	then applying that manifest overwrites the manual scaling that you previously did.
  1134	
  1135	If a [HorizontalPodAutoscaler](/docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale/) (or any
  1136	similar API for horizontal scaling) is managing scaling for a Deployment, don't set `.spec.replicas`.
  1137	
  1138	Instead, allow the Kubernetes
  1139	{{< glossary_tooltip text="control plane" term_id="control-plane" >}} to manage the
  1140	`.spec.replicas` field automatically.
  1141	
  1142	### Selector
  1143	
  1144	`.spec.selector` is a required field that specifies a [label selector](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/)
  1145	for the Pods targeted by this Deployment.
  1146	
  1147	`.spec.selector` must match `.spec.template.metadata.labels`, or it will be rejected by the API.
  1148	
  1149	In API version `apps/v1`, `.spec.selector` and `.metadata.labels` do not default to `.spec.template.metadata.labels` if not set. So they must be set explicitly. Also note that `.spec.selector` is immutable after creation of the Deployment in `apps/v1`.
  1150	
  1151	A Deployment may terminate Pods whose labels match the selector if their template is different
  1152	from `.spec.template` or if the total number of such Pods exceeds `.spec.replicas`. It brings up new
  1153	Pods with `.spec.template` if the number of Pods is less than the desired number.
  1154	
  1155	{{< note >}}
  1156	You should not create other Pods whose labels match this selector, either directly, by creating
  1157	another Deployment, or by creating another controller such as a ReplicaSet or a ReplicationController. If you
  1158	do so, the first Deployment thinks that it created these other Pods. Kubernetes does not stop you from doing this.
  1159	{{< /note >}}
  1160	
  1161	If you have multiple controllers that have overlapping selectors, the controllers will fight with each
  1162	other and won't behave correctly.
  1163	
  1164	### Strategy
  1165	
  1166	`.spec.strategy` specifies the strategy used to replace old Pods by new ones.
  1167	`.spec.strategy.type` can be "Recreate" or "RollingUpdate". "RollingUpdate" is
  1168	the default value.
  1169	
  1170	#### Recreate Deployment
  1171	
  1172	All existing Pods are killed before new ones are created when `.spec.strategy.type==Recreate`.
  1173	
  1174	{{< note >}}
  1175	This will only guarantee Pod termination previous to creation for upgrades. If you upgrade a Deployment, all Pods
  1176	of the old revision will be terminated immediately. Successful removal is awaited before any Pod of the new
  1177	revision is created. If you manually delete a Pod, the lifecycle is controlled by the ReplicaSet and the
  1178	replacement will be created immediately (even if the old Pod is still in a Terminating state). If you need an
  1179	"at most" guarantee for your Pods, you should consider using a
  1180	[StatefulSet](/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset/).

  1188	
  1189	##### Max Unavailable
  1190	
  1191	`.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable` is an optional field that specifies the maximum number
  1192	of Pods that can be unavailable during the update process. The value can be an absolute number (for example, 5)
  1193	or a percentage of desired Pods (for example, 10%). The absolute number is calculated from percentage by
  1194	rounding down. The value cannot be 0 if `.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge` is 0. The default value is 25%.
  1195	
  1196	For example, when this value is set to 30%, the old ReplicaSet can be scaled down to 70% of desired
  1197	Pods immediately when the rolling update starts. Once new Pods are ready, old ReplicaSet can be scaled
  1198	down further, followed by scaling up the new ReplicaSet, ensuring that the total number of Pods available
  1199	at all times during the update is at least 70% of the desired Pods.
  1200	
  1201	##### Max Surge
  1202	
  1203	`.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge` is an optional field that specifies the maximum number of Pods
  1204	that can be created over the desired number of Pods. The value can be an absolute number (for example, 5) or a
  1205	percentage of desired Pods (for example, 10%). The value cannot be 0 if `MaxUnavailable` is 0. The absolute number
  1206	is calculated from the percentage by rounding up. The default value is 25%.
  1207	
  1208	For example, when this value is set to 30%, the new ReplicaSet can be scaled up immediately when the
  1209	rolling update starts, such that the total number of old and new Pods does not exceed 130% of desired
  1210	Pods. Once old Pods have been killed, the new ReplicaSet can be scaled up further, ensuring that the
  1211	total number of Pods running at any time during the update is at most 130% of desired Pods.

90	  from the resource metrics API for each Pod targeted by the HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
    91	  Then, if a target utilization value is set, the controller calculates the utilization
    92	  value as a percentage of the equivalent
    93	  [resource request](/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/#requests-and-limits)
    94	  on the containers in each Pod. If a target raw value is set, the raw metric values are used directly.
    95	  The controller then takes the mean of the utilization or the raw value (depending on the type
    96	  of target specified) across all targeted Pods, and produces a ratio used to scale
    97	  the number of desired replicas.
    98	
    99	  Please note that if some of the Pod's containers do not have the relevant resource request set,
   100	  CPU utilization for the Pod will not be defined and the autoscaler will
   101	  not take any action for that metric. See the [algorithm details](#algorithm-details) section below
   102	  for more information about how the autoscaling algorithm works.
   103	
   104	- For per-pod custom metrics, the controller functions similarly to per-pod resource metrics,
   105	  except that it works with raw values, not utilization values.
   106	
   107	- For object metrics and external metrics, a single metric is fetched, which describes
   108	  the object in question. This metric is compared to the target
   109	  value, to produce a ratio as above. In the `autoscaling/v2` API
   110	  version, this value can optionally be divided by the number of Pods before the
   111	  comparison is made.
   112	
   113	The common use for HorizontalPodAutoscaler is to configure it to fetch metrics from
   114	{{< glossary_tooltip text="aggregated APIs" term_id="aggregation-layer" >}}
   115	(`metrics.k8s.io`, `custom.metrics.k8s.io`, or `external.metrics.k8s.io`). The `metrics.k8s.io` API is
   116	usually provided by an add-on named Metrics Server, which needs to be launched separately.
   117	For more information about resource metrics, see
   118	[Metrics Server](/docs/tasks/debug/debug-cluster/resource-metrics-pipeline/#metrics-server).
   119	
   120	[Support for metrics APIs](#support-for-metrics-apis) explains the stability guarantees and support status for these
   121	different APIs.
   122	
   123	The HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller accesses corresponding workload resources that support scaling (such as Deployments
   124	and StatefulSet). These resources each have a subresource named `scale`, an interface that allows you to dynamically set the
   125	number of replicas and examine each of their current states.
   126	For general information about subresources in the Kubernetes API, see
   127	[Kubernetes API Concepts](/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/).
   128	
   129	### Algorithm details
   130	
   131	From the most basic perspective, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller
   132	operates on the ratio between desired metric value and current metric
   133	value:
   134	
   135	```math
   136	\begin{equation*}
   137	desiredReplicas = ceil\left\lceil currentReplicas \times \frac{currentMetricValue}{desiredMetricValue} \right\rceil
   138	\end{equation*}
   139	```
   140	
   141	For example, if the current metric value is `200m`, and the desired value
   142	is `100m`, the number of replicas will be doubled, since
   143	\\( { 200.0 \div 100.0 } = 2.0 \\).  
   144	If the current value is instead `50m`, you'll halve the number of

   243	## How Kubernetes applies resource requests and limits {#how-pods-with-resource-limits-are-run}
   244	
   245	When the kubelet starts a container as part of a Pod, the kubelet passes that container's
   246	requests and limits for memory and CPU to the container runtime.
   247	
   248	On Linux, the container runtime typically configures
   249	kernel {{< glossary_tooltip text="cgroups" term_id="cgroup" >}} that apply and enforce the
   250	limits you defined.
   251	
   252	- The CPU limit defines a hard ceiling on how much CPU time the container can use.
   253	  During each scheduling interval (time slice), the Linux kernel checks to see if this
   254	  limit is exceeded; if so, the kernel waits before allowing that cgroup to resume execution.
   255	- The CPU request typically defines a weighting. If several different containers (cgroups)
   256	  want to run on a contended system, workloads with larger CPU requests are allocated more
   257	  CPU time than workloads with small requests.
   258	- The memory request is mainly used during (Kubernetes) Pod scheduling. On a node that uses
   259	  cgroups v2, the container runtime might use the memory request as a hint to set
   260	  `memory.min` and `memory.low`.
   261	- The memory limit defines a memory limit for that cgroup. If the container tries to
   262	  allocate more memory than this limit, the Linux kernel out-of-memory subsystem activates
   263	  and, typically, intervenes by stopping one of the processes in the container that tried
   264	  to allocate memory. If that process is the container's PID 1, and the container is marked
   265	  as restartable, Kubernetes restarts the container.
   266	- The memory limit for the Pod or container can also apply to pages in memory backed
   267	  volumes, such as an `emptyDir`. The kubelet tracks `tmpfs` emptyDir volumes as container
   268	  memory use, rather than as local ephemeral storage.　When using memory backed `emptyDir`,
   269	  be sure to check the notes [below](#memory-backed-emptydir).
   270

   272	memory overall, it is likely that the Pod the container belongs to will be
   273	{{< glossary_tooltip text="evicted" term_id="eviction" >}}.
   274	
   275	A container might or might not be allowed to exceed its CPU limit for extended periods of time.
   276	However, container runtimes don't terminate Pods or containers for excessive CPU usage.

   279	see the [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting) section.

   283	The kubelet reports the resource usage of a Pod as part of the Pod

1	---
     2	reviewers:
     3	- thockin
     4	- caseydavenport
     5	- danwinship
     6	title: Network Policies
     7	content_type: concept
     8	api_metadata:
     9	- apiVersion: "networking.k8s.io/v1"
    10	  kind: "NetworkPolicy"
    11	weight: 70
    12	description: >-
    13	  If you want to control traffic flow at the IP address or port level (OSI layer 3 or 4),
    14	  NetworkPolicies allow you to specify rules for traffic flow within your cluster, and
    15	  also between Pods and the outside world.
    16	  Your cluster must use a network plugin that supports NetworkPolicy enforcement.
    17	---
    18	
    19	<!-- overview -->
    20	
    21	If you want to control traffic flow at the IP address or port level for TCP, UDP, and SCTP protocols,
    22	then you might consider using Kubernetes NetworkPolicies for particular applications in your cluster.
    23	NetworkPolicies are an application-centric construct which allow you to specify how a
    24	{{< glossary_tooltip text="pod" term_id="pod">}} is allowed to communicate with various network
    25	"entities" (we use the word "entity" here to avoid overloading the more common terms such as
    26	"endpoints" and "services", which have specific Kubernetes connotations) over the network.
    27	NetworkPolicies apply to a connection with a pod on one or both ends, and are not relevant to
    28	other connections.
    29	
    30	The entities that a Pod can communicate with are identified through a combination of the following
    31	three identifiers:
    32	
    33	1. Other pods that are allowed (exception: a pod cannot block access to itself)
    34	1. Namespaces that are allowed
    35	1. IP blocks (exception: traffic to and from the node where a Pod is running is always allowed,
    36	   regardless of the IP address of the Pod or the node)
    37	
    38	When defining a pod- or namespace-based NetworkPolicy, you use a
    39	{{< glossary_tooltip text="selector" term_id="selector">}} to specify what traffic is allowed to
    40	and from the Pod(s) that match the selector.
    41	
    42	Meanwhile, when IP-based NetworkPolicies are created, we define policies based on IP blocks (CIDR ranges).
    43	
    44	<!-- body -->
    45	## Prerequisites
    46	
    47	Network policies are implemented by the [network plugin](/docs/concepts/extend-kubernetes/compute-storage-net/network-plugins/).
    48	To use network policies, you must be using a networking solution which supports NetworkPolicy.
    49	Creating a NetworkPolicy resource without a controller that implements it will have no effect.
    50	
    51	## The two sorts of pod isolation
    52	
    53	There are two sorts of isolation for a pod: isolation for egress, and isolation for ingress.
    54	They concern what connections may be established. "Isolation" here is not absolute, rather it
    55	means "some restrictions apply". The alternative, "non-isolated for $direction", means that no
    56	restrictions apply in the stated direction. The two sorts of isolation (or not) are declared
    57	independently, and are both relevant for a connection from one pod to another.
    58	
    59	By default, a pod is non-isolated for egress; all outbound connections are allowed.
    60	A pod is isolated for egress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and has
    61	"Egress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for egress.
    62	When a pod is isolated for egress, the only allowed connections from the pod are those allowed by
    63	the `egress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to the pod for egress. Reply traffic for those
    64	allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
    65	The effects of those `egress` lists combine additively.
    66	
    67	By default, a pod is non-isolated for ingress; all inbound connections are allowed.
    68	A pod is isolated for ingress if there is any NetworkPolicy that both selects the pod and
    69	has "Ingress" in its `policyTypes`; we say that such a policy applies to the pod for ingress.
    70	When a pod is isolated for ingress, the only allowed connections into the pod are those from
    71	the pod's node and those allowed by the `ingress` list of some NetworkPolicy that applies to
    72	the pod for ingress. Reply traffic for those allowed connections will also be implicitly allowed.
    73	The effects of those `ingress` lists combine additively.
    74	
    75	Network policies do not conflict; they are additive. If any policy or policies apply to a given
    76	pod for a given direction, the connections allowed in that direction from that pod is the union of
    77	what the applicable policies allow. Thus, order of evaluation does not affect the policy result.
    78	
    79	For a connection from a source pod to a destination pod to be allowed, both the egress policy on
    80	the source pod and the ingress policy on the destination pod need to allow the connection. If
    81	either side does not allow the connection, it will not happen.
    82	
    83	## The NetworkPolicy resource {#networkpolicy-resource}
    84	
    85	See the [NetworkPolicy](/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/{{< param "version" >}}/#networkpolicy-v1-networking-k8s-io)
    86	reference for a full definition of the resource.
    87	
    88	An example NetworkPolicy might look like this:
    89	
    90	{{% code_sample file="service/networking/networkpolicy.yaml" %}}
    91	
    92	{{< note >}}
    93	POSTing this to the API server for your cluster will have no effect unless your chosen networking
    94	solution supports network policy.
    95	{{< /note >}}
    96	
    97	__Mandatory Fields__: As with all other Kubernetes config, a NetworkPolicy needs `apiVersion`,
    98	`kind`, and `metadata` fields. For general information about working with config files, see
    99	[Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap](/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-pod-configmap/),
   100	and [Object Management](/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/object-management).
   101	
   102	**spec**: NetworkPolicy [spec](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md#spec-and-status)
   103	has all the information needed to define a particular network policy in the given namespace.
   104	
   105	**podSelector**: Each NetworkPolicy includes a `podSelector` which selects the grouping of pods to
   106	which the policy applies. The example policy selects pods with the label "role=db". An empty
   107	`podSelector` selects all pods in the namespace.
   108	
   109	**policyTypes**: Each NetworkPolicy includes a `policyTypes` list which may include either
   110	`Ingress`, `Egress`, or both. The `policyTypes` field indicates whether or not the given policy
